cards.prompt: What is the primary memory difference between two OS processes versus two threads within the same process?
cards.answer: Processes have isolated virtual address spaces; threads share the same heap and global address space while maintaining separate stacks and registers
accepted_answers: threads share memory processes are isolated
processes have separate address spaces threads share heap
cards.explanation: A context switch between processes requires switching page tables (flushing TLB), whereas threads share virtual memory mappings and only swap stack pointers and CPU registers.

cards.prompt: Why can a Mutex only be unlocked by the thread that locked it, whereas a Binary Semaphore can be signaled by any thread or ISR?
cards.answer: Mutexes enforce strict ownership (enabling priority inheritance), while semaphores are ownership-agnostic signaling primitives
accepted_answers: mutex has ownership semaphore does not
cards.explanation: Because a Mutex tracks its owning thread, the OS kernel can temporarily boost the owner's priority if a higher-priority thread blocks on it (preventing unbounded priority inversion).

cards.prompt: What are the four Coffman conditions that must ALL hold simultaneously for a deadlock to occur?
cards.answer: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait
accepted_answers: mutual exclusion hold and wait no preemption circular wait
cards.explanation: Breaking any single condition—most commonly enforcing a global lock acquisition ordering to break Circular Wait—mathematically prevents deadlocks.

cards.prompt: What hardware unit inside the CPU translates virtual memory addresses into physical RAM addresses using page tables?
cards.explanation: The MMU enforces per-page read/write/execute permissions and caches recent translations in the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB).

cards.prompt: What happens when a process accesses a virtual page whose Page Table Entry (PTE) has its Present/Valid bit set to 0?
cards.answer: A Page Fault exception is triggered in the CPU
cards.explanation: The OS page fault handler checks whether the access is valid (e.g., demand paging or copy-on-write) to map a physical frame, or terminates the process with SIGSEGV if invalid.

cards.prompt: Why does a Condition Variable (`std::condition_variable` / `pthread_cond_wait`) ALWAYS require a `while` loop around `wait()` instead of an `if` statement?
cards.answer: To guard against spurious wakeups and stolen conditions where another thread modified the predicate before the woken thread re-acquired the mutex
cards.explanation: OS schedulers may wake a thread waiting on a condition variable without a signal, or another consumer may consume the item before the woken thread locks the mutex.

cards.prompt: In C++11/20 `std::atomic`, what guarantee does a Release-Acquire (`memory_order_release` / `memory_order_acquire`) pair provide across two threads?
cards.answer: All memory writes performed by Thread A before the atomic store-release become visible to Thread B after the atomic load-acquire
accepted_answers: writes before release are visible after acquire
cards.explanation: Release-Acquire prevents compiler and CPU instruction reordering across the atomic boundary without paying the full hardware barrier cost of `seq_cst` on weak memory architectures like ARM.

cards.prompt: What is 'False Sharing' in multi-core systems and how do you fix it in C++17?
cards.answer: Two threads on different cores modify independent variables that sit on the same 64-byte CPU cache line, causing cache invalidation ping-pong; fix with `alignas(64)`
accepted_answers: independent variables sharing a cache line
cards.explanation: Hardware cache coherence protocols (MESI) track ownership at cache-line granularity (typically 64 bytes), so padding or `alignas(std::hardware_destructive_interference_size)` eliminates contention.

cards.prompt: What is a Zombie process (`Z` state) in Linux and how is it cleaned up?
cards.answer: A terminated process whose exit status has not yet been read by its parent via `wait()` or `waitpid()`
accepted_answers: terminated process waiting for parent to call wait
cards.explanation: A zombie uses zero RAM or CPU—only a PID slot in the kernel process table—until its parent reaps it (or init/systemd adopts and reaps it if the parent dies).

cards.prompt: What is the 'ABA Problem' in lock-free Compare-And-Swap (CAS) algorithms?
cards.answer: A shared location changes from A to B and back to A while a thread is preempted, tricking CAS into thinking nothing changed
accepted_answers: value changes A to B to A fooling CAS
cards.explanation: If A is a freed and reallocated pointer, CAS succeeds even though the underlying node's next-pointer structure changed; tagged pointers or hazard pointers prevent it.

cards.prompt: In Rate-Monotonic Scheduling (RMS) for periodic real-time tasks, how are static priorities assigned?
cards.answer: Tasks with shorter periods (higher execution frequency) receive higher static priority
cards.explanation: RMS is optimal among fixed-priority preemptive schedulers and guarantees schedulability if total CPU utilization is <= n*(2^(1/n) - 1) (~69.3% as n -> infinity).

cards.prompt: Why does calling `fork()` in Linux not immediately duplicate all physical RAM pages of a large parent process?
cards.answer: Copy-on-Write (CoW) shares read-only physical pages between parent and child until either process attempts a write
cards.explanation: CoW makes `fork()` followed by `execve()` nearly instantaneous because physical memory pages are only copied on demand when modified.

cards.prompt: When is a Spinlock preferable over a sleeping Mutex?
cards.answer: On multi-core systems when the critical section is extremely short (fewer cycles than two context switches) and sleeping is forbidden (e.g., inside an ISR)
accepted_answers: very short critical sections on multicore or in ISRs
cards.explanation: Never use a spinlock on a single-core CPU with preemption disabled—the spinning thread will monopolize the sole core forever while the lock holder cannot run.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between Internal Fragmentation and External Fragmentation?
cards.answer: Internal is wasted unused bytes inside an allocated fixed-size block/page; External is free memory broken into non-contiguous holes too small to satisfy a large request
accepted_answers: internal is inside allocated blocks external is between blocks
cards.explanation: Fixed-block memory pools eliminate external fragmentation completely in safety-critical embedded systems at the cost of minor internal fragmentation.

cards.prompt: Which Linux Inter-Process Communication (IPC) mechanism provides the lowest latency and highest throughput for bulk sensor frames?
cards.answer: POSIX Shared Memory (`shm_open` + `mmap`) paired with atomics or semaphores
cards.explanation: Unlike pipes or sockets, shared memory avoids copying payloads twice through kernel space (zero-copy between processes).
